1303.title: Rama is born in spring
1303.hook: Krishna calls spring his season, and in spring Rama is born: why Hindus throw God a birthday
1303.carry: avatar: god takes birth among us
1303.tomorrow: why does God catch a fever in summer?
1303.howItsDone: On Rama Navami, in the spring month of Chaitra, many Hindu temples and homes mark Rama's birth around midday with a cradle, songs and sweets, and many devotees keep a fast; people who follow Ayurveda also eat lighter and move more as the spring thaw begins.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Agni was fed well: eating is an offering to the fire within, and winter's fire burns strong.

Of the seasons, I am the one that brings flowers. That's Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita, paraphrased, naming the places his glory shows, and among the seasons he picks spring. Ayurveda's Charaka reads the same season more plainly: winter's heaviness thaws, so eat lighter and move more. But Hindus remember spring for something bigger. In the spring month of Chaitra, in Ayodhya, an old king who waited years for a child finally hears a baby cry. Today, spring, and the birth of Rama.
screen: `OF SEASONS, I AM SPRING.` → `CHARAKA: THE THAW.` → `A BABY CRIES IN AYODHYA.`

segments.voice: The story is in Valmiki's Ramayana. King Dasharatha has everything but a son, and he grows old waiting. So he holds a great fire sacrifice. Out of the fire, the poem says, rises a shining being carrying a golden vessel of payasa, sweet rice cooked in milk, a gift from the gods, and Dasharatha shares it among his three queens. Meanwhile the gods have a problem. The demon king Ravana is protected by a boon: no god or demon can kill him. He never thought to ask for safety from a human. So Vishnu agrees to be born as one. And in Chaitra, on the ninth day of the bright half of the month, Queen Kausalya gives birth to Rama. Here's the teaching, plainly: avatar, God coming down. Hindus believe God takes birth in the world, again and again, when it needs setting right. Krishna says it in the Gita, paraphrased: whenever dharma falls and wrong rises, I come into being, age after age. And notice how Rama arrives. Not as a blaze in the sky, but as a baby who has to be fed and held. So every spring Hindus keep Rama Navami, the ninth. Many temples mark the birth around midday, rock a small cradle, sing and share sweets. A birthday party for God sounds strange until you see the point: God came close enough to be born into a family.
screen: `PAYASA FROM THE FIRE` · `RAVANA'S BOON, VISHNU'S BIRTH` · `AVATAR: GOD COMES DOWN` · `RAMA NAVAMI: A CRADLE AT MIDDAY`

segments.voice: Sit tall and let three slow breaths come and go. Then picture something newly born in your life this season, a plant, a plan, a baby in the family, and hold it in mind the way you'd hold an infant: gently, with both hands. If you pray, say Rama's name softly a few times, as many Hindus do. If you don't, simply rest in the welcome.
The seasons. In spring, Charaka's thaw and the Gita's flowers, and the Hindu year's great spring birth: Rama, God born as a child in the month of Chaitra. Today's word.
Your line: avatar, God takes birth among us. That's why Rama Navami is a birthday. See you tomorrow.

1304.title: Jagannath's summer fever
1304.hook: every summer, after a grand bath, the god of Puri falls ill and is nursed out of sight: why Hindus serve God like family
1304.carry: murti seva: god is cared for like family
1304.tomorrow: who holds the hill when it rains?
1304.howItsDone: At Puri, Jagannath, Balabhadra and Subhadra are bathed on Snana Purnima and then rest out of public sight for about two weeks, nursed with herbal medicines; in summer many Hindu families dress their home deity in light cotton and offer cooling food and water. People who follow Ayurveda keep cool with sweet, cool, liquid food and rest.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rama was born in spring: avatar, God takes birth among us, kept every year as Rama Navami.

The hottest month of the year in Puri, on India's east coast. On the full moon, the temple's three great wooden deities, Jagannath, his brother Balabhadra and his sister Subhadra, are carried out to a high platform in front of huge crowds and bathed with pot after pot of cool water. It's a loud, joyful day. And then, tradition says, they catch a fever. Today, the god who gets sick in summer.
screen: `THE HOTTEST MONTH, IN PURI.` → `A BATH IN FRONT OF THE CROWDS.` → `AND THEN, A FEVER.`

segments.voice: After the bathing festival, Snana Purnima, the temple's inner doors close to the public for about two weeks. In Puri's tradition this is anasara: the deities are said to be unwell, and they rest out of sight. Their own hereditary servants nurse them with herbal medicines and simple offerings instead of the usual feasts, until they recover. Then they appear again, freshly painted, and soon after ride out in their great chariots for the Ratha Yatra. Charaka would recognize the care. His summer chapter says the strong sun draws moisture out of the body, so you meet it with cool water, light food and rest. But the teaching here is bigger than health. Hindus treat a consecrated image, a murti, not as a statue but as a presence: God invited in and served the way you'd serve a beloved guest or a family member. So the deity is woken in the morning, bathed, dressed, fed, and put to rest at night, and in Puri, even nursed through a fever. That's murti seva, service to God in the image. You see it in ordinary homes too. In summer many families dress their home deity in light cotton, offer cooling food and water, and some set a small fan by the shrine. To an outsider it can look like pretend. To a devotee it's love that pays attention, the way you'd notice a grandparent getting too warm. In this teaching God isn't only far away. He's close enough to be looked after.
screen: `SNANA PURNIMA, THEN ANASARA` · `RATHA YATRA AND SUMMER CARE` · `MURTI SEVA: GOD SERVED LIKE FAMILY` · `COTTON CLOTHES AND A SMALL FAN`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to the tip of the nose and notice that the in-breath is a little cooler there than the out-breath; rest on the cool of each inhale. Then picture one small act of care you could give today, a glass of cold water, a fan turned toward someone. If you pray, offer a little water at your family's shrine, as many Hindus do in the heat. If you don't, offer it to someone thirsty.
The seasons. In summer, Charaka's sun draws moisture out and cool water puts it back, and in Puri, God himself is bathed, rests and is nursed through the heat. Today's word.

1305.title: Krishna lifts the hill
1305.hook: Indra sends a week of rain, and a boy lifts a hill over the village: why Hindus speak of taking refuge in God
1305.carry: sharanagati: take refuge, and god holds the hill
1305.tomorrow: why does Krishna vanish from the dance?
1305.howItsDone: Hindus remember Krishna lifting Govardhan at Govardhan Puja, the day after Diwali, often with a mountain of food (Annakut); many Vaishnavas take refuge with the words Shri Krishna sharanam mama, and some keep vows through the rainy months of Chaturmas. People who follow Ayurveda eat light and keep dry in the rains.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jagannath was nursed through his summer fever: murti seva, God is cared for like family.

The first rain on dry ground has a smell, and it often arrives to cheering. Somebody fries pakoras. Charaka adds a gentle note: in the rains your inner fire burns low, so eat light, drink clean water, keep your feet dry and go easy. Now imagine rain that doesn't stop. Seven days of it, sent on purpose, by an angry god. Today, the rains, and the hill that became an umbrella.
screen: `THE FIRST RAIN. PAKORAS.` → `CHARAKA: THE FIRE BURNS LOW.` → `SEVEN DAYS OF RAIN.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Bhagavata Purana. In the cowherd village of Vraja, everyone is preparing the yearly offering to Indra, king of the gods and lord of rain. The boy Krishna asks his father why. Our living comes from this hill, he says, from the cows and the forest; let's honor Govardhan instead. They do, and Indra is furious. He sends clouds that pour rain and hail on the village, with wind tearing at the cattle sheds. The people and the cows run to Krishna. And Krishna, with one hand, lifts Govardhan Hill and holds it up like an umbrella. Come under, he tells them, all of you, with your cows. For seven days, the text says, he holds it without moving, while the whole village shelters. In the Bhagavata, Krishna gives his reason, paraphrased: these people have taken me as their refuge, and protecting them is my vow. That's the teaching, plainly: sharanagati, taking refuge in God, a central idea in Hindu devotion. You don't earn shelter by being strong. You come under. And notice what Krishna doesn't do. He doesn't stop the storm. The rain keeps falling for seven days; he holds a roof over everyone through it. Many teachers read that as the shape of refuge: not a life with no storms, but someone holding the hill. Hindus remember it every year at Govardhan Puja, the day after Diwali, often with a heaped mountain of food. And in the rainy months, Chaturmas, many Hindus keep vows, and wandering monks stop traveling and stay in one place, the way the village stayed under the hill.
screen: `HONOR THE HILL, NOT INDRA` · `ONE HAND HOLDS GOVARDHAN` · `SHARANAGATI: COME UNDER` · `GOVARDHAN PUJA AND CHATURMAS`

segments.voice: Let sounds come and go like rain on a roof, and decide that for this sit you won't go anywhere, not even in your head to the next thing. Picture a roof over you that you didn't build. If you pray, say Shri Krishna sharanam mama, Krishna is my refuge, as many Vaishnavas do, once, and rest under it. If you don't, simply let yourself be sheltered for a few breaths.
The seasons. In the rains, Charaka's low fire asks us to go easy, and the Bhagavata's seven-day storm shows Krishna holding the hill over everyone who came to him. Today's word.
Your line: sharanagati, take refuge, and God holds the hill. The rain may keep falling. I'll be here tomorrow.

1306.title: Krishna vanishes from the dance
1306.hook: on autumn's moonlit nights the gopis dance with Krishna, grow proud, and he's gone: the Hindu teaching on the ego
1306.carry: ahankara: pride hides god, longing brings him back
1306.howItsDone: On Sharad Purnima, autumn's full moon, many Hindus remember Krishna's raas with the gopis, and some families leave rice cooked in milk under the moon overnight; people who follow Ayurveda cool the body in autumn with sweet and bitter foods, ghee and early-night moonlight.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna held Govardhan through seven days of storm: sharanagati, take refuge, and God holds the hill.

Autumn, in Charaka's year, is a jolt: the clouds clear, the sun comes out hard after the rains, and his advice turns to cooling food and moonlight early in the night. Hindus give autumn its own full moon, Sharad Purnima, and in some homes a bowl of rice and milk is left out under it overnight. The Bhagavata Purana sets its most famous night in this season too. Autumn nights, jasmine in bloom, the moon coming up. And from the forest, a flute.
screen: `AUTUMN: A SUDDEN SUN.` → `RICE AND MILK UNDER THE MOON.` → `FROM THE FOREST, A FLUTE.`

segments.voice: When the gopis, the cowherd women of Vraja, hear Krishna's flute, they drop everything. One leaves milk on the fire. One leaves her meal half eaten. They run to the forest, and Krishna plays and dances with them by the Yamuna in the moonlight. Then, the Bhagavata says, the gopis begin to feel proud. Each thinks, of all the women in the world, I'm the one he chose. And Krishna disappears. Just like that, the circle is empty. The gopis search the forest, asking the trees and vines if they've seen him. They act out his childhood to feel near him. At last they sit by the river and sing, simply longing for him, and Krishna returns and stands among them. Only then does the great circle dance begin: the raas. The text says plainly why he left: to take away their pride. That's the teaching: ahankara, the ego, literally the I-maker. In Hindu thought it's the sense of me and mine that stands between us and God, and Krishna's vanishing shows it can creep in even through love. The gopis didn't lose him by loving too much. They lost him when the love turned into, look at me. He came back when it turned into longing again. That's why bhakti teachers hold up the gopis as the great devotees: not because they never got proud, but because they never stopped longing. Autumn still carries the dance. Many Hindus remember the raas on Sharad Purnima, and the circle dances of the autumn festivals share its name.
screen: `THE FLUTE: THEY DROP EVERYTHING` · `HE VANISHES; THEY LONG FOR HIM` · `AHANKARA: THE I-MAKER` · `LONGING BRINGS HIM BACK`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath be cool and easy, like an autumn evening. Notice the little voice that narrates you: how am I doing, am I good at this. Don't fight it. Just see it, and each time, come back to the breath. If you pray, sing or say one name of Krishna, the way the gopis sang by the river. If you don't, sit in plain thanks for the turning year.

1307.title: Bhrigu finds food is Brahman
1307.hook: a young man asks his father what Brahman is, and the first answer he finds is food
1307.carry: food is brahman: never speak ill of it
1307.howItsDone: In Hindu homes that keep these customs, food is offered before it is eaten, and complaining about food or wasting it is avoided, a stance the Taittiriya Upanishad puts as a vow not to speak ill of food.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Krishna vanished from the dance: ahankara, pride hides God, and longing brings him back.

A son goes to his father with one request. Teach me Brahman, he says: the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. His name is Bhrigu. His father is Varuna. And Varuna doesn't lecture. He gives a riddle and sends him away to work it out. Bhrigu goes off, sits with it, practices, and comes back with an answer that might seem almost too ordinary for the question. He says: food. A run of days on food as practice starts with that answer.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `A RIDDLE, NOT A LECTURE.` → `THE FIRST ANSWER: FOOD.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Varuna's riddle, paraphrased: that from which beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they return, seek to know that. That is Brahman. And one instruction: seek it through tapas, disciplined, inward effort. So Bhrigu does, and he comes to see, the text says, that food is Brahman. From food beings are born. By food they live. Into food they return. It fits every line of the riddle. Now the twist. Varuna doesn't say, well done, you're finished. He gives the same instruction again, seek it through tapas, and sends him out once more. Step by step Bhrigu goes deeper: to breath, to mind, to understanding, and at last to bliss. Three things. First, food isn't thrown away when he goes deeper. It's the first floor of the house, and the house stands on it. Second, the Upanishad draws vows out of it. Do not speak ill of food. Do not despise food. Make much food. Not diet rules but a stance: food handled with respect, because it was the first thing Bhrigu found holy. Third, the Ayurvedic texts arrive somewhere close from another direction. Charaka treats food as what sustains the life of living beings, the ground health is built on, which is why these days give food a whole week. So food as practice doesn't start with a rule about what to eat. It starts with seeing what food is.

1308.title: Kunti's half for Bhima
1308.hook: in hiding, a mother splits the begged food in two, half for one son: the Gita's middle way of eating

1308.tomorrow: who is eating when you eat?
1308.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda eat in measure, the amount their own digestion handles well, leaving some room rather than eating until full; many Hindus keep fasts such as Ekadashi with fruit and milk, in the spirit of the Gita's measured eating.

The five Pandava brothers are in hiding, dressed as poor brahmins, living on what they can beg in a small town called Ekachakra. Every evening they bring the food home to their mother, Kunti, and she divides it. Not in six equal shares. She splits it in two. Half goes to one son, Bhima. The other half she shares among the rest of them and herself. It sounds unfair, until you meet Bhima. Today, the measure.
screen: `IN HIDING, LIVING ON ALMS.` → `KUNTI SPLITS IT IN TWO.` → `HALF FOR BHIMA.`

segments.voice: Bhima is the strongest of the brothers, and the Mahabharata gives him a nickname, Vrikodara, wolf-belly, for his enormous hunger. Kunti isn't playing favorites. She's feeding each son by what he needs. Ayurveda has a word for that: matra, measure. Charaka's chapter on the daily round begins, paraphrased: one should eat in measure, and the measure depends on the strength of your own digestive fire. Bhima's fire is huge. Yours may not be. Charaka even gives a picture: fill the stomach's room in three parts, one with food, one with drink, and leave one for the body's own workings. Don't fill it to the top. Now the Hindu teaching that makes this more than a diet. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna tells Arjuna, paraphrased, that yoga isn't for the one who eats too much, nor for the one who doesn't eat at all. It's for the one who is yukta, measured, balanced, in eating and rest, in sleeping and waking, in work. For that person, he says, yoga ends sorrow. Notice both edges are ruled out. Stuffing yourself is out, and so is starving yourself to look holy. That's why Hindu fasts, at their best, are kept with care, often with fruit and milk, and why a grandmother keeping Ekadashi will still make sure you eat. The measure isn't a number handed down from outside. It's yours, and finding it is part of the spiritual path, as Kunti knew when she gave Bhima half.
screen: `VRIKODARA: WOLF-BELLY` · `MATRA: MEASURE BY YOUR OWN FIRE` · `YUKTA: MEASURED, BALANCED` · `NOT TOO MUCH, NOT TOO LITTLE`

segments.voice: Rest a hand on your stomach if you like, and ask quietly: empty, part-full, or full? Answer with what's there, not with a judgment, and feel the breath moving under your hand. If you pray, offer the next meal before it comes, as many Hindus do. If you don't, simply promise to notice when it's enough.
Food as practice. Matra and yukta: measure set by your own fire, and the Gita's middle way, neither too much nor too little. Today's word.

A phone propped against a water glass, a video playing, a fork going up and down on its own. Now a very old scene. Five learned householders, with a famous teacher, go to King Ashvapati with one question: what is the Self that is in everyone, the universal fire? He tells them to come back in the morning. And when he answers, the answer ends at the dinner plate. Today, the way of eating.
screen: `A PHONE AGAINST A WATER GLASS.` → `SIX SEEKERS AT A KING’S DOOR.` → `THE ANSWER ENDS AT THE PLATE.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Chandogya Upanishad. King Ashvapati asks each guest what he worships as the Self. One says the sky, one the sun, one the wind, one space, one water, one the earth. Each, the king says, has hold of a piece. The whole is Vaishvanara, the fire that belongs to all people: the one Self, the same fire in everything and in you. Then he makes it practical. When food comes, he says, paraphrased, the first bite is an offering. Offer it to prana, the breath of life, saying svaha, as if into a sacred fire, and the next bites to the other breaths, five in all. Eat that way, the Upanishad says, and your meal becomes a fire offering that satisfies the whole world. Here's the teaching, plainly: the fire that digests your food is not just chemistry. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says, paraphrased: I become the fire Vaishvanara, living in the bodies of beings, and with the breath I digest food. So in Hindu teaching, eating is worship, and God is the fire that receives the meal. That's why some Hindu families, before eating, sprinkle water around the plate and offer five tiny morsels with pranaya svaha. And it's why Charaka's rules for eating sound like temple rules: warm food, after the last meal is digested, in a pleasant place, not too fast or too slow, without talking and laughing through it, with your mind on the food. You don't scroll through an offering.
screen: `SIX PIECES, ONE FIRE` · `THE FIRST BITE: PRANAYA SVAHA` · `GOD, THE FIRE THAT RECEIVES` · `YOU DON’T SCROLL THROUGH AN OFFERING`

segments.voice: If there's water or tea near you, pick it up, feel its weight and its warmth or cool, and take one sip, holding it a moment before you follow it down; if nothing's at hand, do the same with a breath. Then sit with whatever is left: the taste, the warmth, the quiet. If you pray, offer that first sip silently, the way some Hindus offer the first bite: to the breath of life, svaha. If you don't, simply let the first sip be fully noticed.
Food as practice. Vaishvanara, the one fire in everything, digesting your food: so the Upanishad makes the first bite an offering, and Charaka asks you to eat with your mind on it. Today's word.
